text: When something breaks on a Linux server, guessing wastes time — the system has already written down exactly what happened, in plain text. Getting comfortable with where Linux keeps its logs, and how to search through them quickly under pressure, is one of the single highest-leverage administration skills there is.

Since systemd manages services, it also centralizes their logs into the journal. journalctl -u nginx shows everything that service has logged, -f follows it live the same way tail -f does, and --since lets you filter by time instead of scrolling through everything. For any systemd service, that's the fastest way to see exactly what it's been doing.

Alongside the journal, Linux keeps plain-text files under /var/log/. syslog, or messages on RHEL-based systems, is the general log — kernel messages, background services, anything not sent somewhere more specific. auth.log, or secure on RHEL-based systems, is specifically authentication activity: every SSH login, every sudo command. That's the file you check first for anything security-related.

tail -f watches a log live, showing new lines as they're written — leave it running while you try to reproduce a problem. grep filters a log down to just the lines matching a pattern. Piping tail's output into grep, to pull failed SSH logins out of the auth log for example, is one of the most common combinations in Linux troubleshooting.

Put it together and most investigations follow the same three steps: systemctl status to check if the service is even running, journalctl -u to see what it's logged recently, then the system-wide syslog if the service itself looks healthy but something underneath it isn't. Start specific, then go broad.

Most problems — a crash on startup, a typo in a config file, a port already in use — show up clearly in the first two steps. Next up: turning the commands from this whole chapter into reusable shell scripts, so you're not retyping them by hand every time.
